title: Stephen Kleene (CS 360 Theory of Computing Hall of Fame)
version: University of Waterloo CS 360 course page, viewed 2026-10-13
why: Concise, readable attribution of the notion of regular expression to Kleene's 1956 Automata Studies paper, used because the primary Kleene PDFs are scanned or blocked.

locator: abstract, p. 419 (scanned CACM copy; line-break hyphen in 'produces' rejoined)
claim: Thompson's 1968 compiler accepted a regular expression as its source language and produced an IBM 7094 program as its object language.
quote: The compiler accepts a regular expression as source language and produces an IBM 7094 program as object language.

claim: Thompson's regular expression implementation was for his QED editor running on CTSS.
quote: Thompson's regular expression implementation was for his QED editor running on the CTSS

claim: Thompson's construction creates exactly one NFA state per character or metacharacter in the regex, excluding parentheses, so the number of NFA states is at most the length of the regex.
quote: this technique creates exactly one state per character or metacharacter in the regular expression, excluding parentheses. Therefore the number of states in the final NFA is at most equal to the length of the original regular expression.

claim: For a regular expression of length m run on text of length n, the Thompson NFA simulation requires O(mn) time.
quote: For a regular expression of length m run on text of length n, the Thompson NFA requires O(mn) time.

claim: On the regex a?^n a^n matched against a^n (n = 29), Perl requires over sixty seconds while the Thompson NFA requires twenty microseconds.
quote: Notice that Perl requires over sixty seconds to match a 29-character string. The other approach, labeled Thompson NFA for reasons that will be explained later, requires twenty microseconds to match the string.

claim: Perl, PCRE, Python and Ruby use recursive backtracking, and PCRE stops getting the right answer at n=23 because it aborts the recursion after a maximum number of steps.
quote: From the graph it is clear that Perl, PCRE, Python, and Ruby are all using recursive backtracking. PCRE stops getting the right answer at n=23, because it aborts the recursive backtracking after a maximum number of steps.

claim: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott introduced non-deterministic finite automata and the concept of non-determinism in 1959.
quote: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott introduced non-deterministic finite automata and the concept of non-determinism in 1959

claim: In a 1956 paper, Kleene introduced the notion of regular expression and proved that regular-expression languages and finite-automata languages are the same class (Kleene's Theorem).
quote: In a 1956 paper, Kleene introduced the notion of regular expression, and proved that the languages specified by regular expressions and the languages generated by finite automata constituted the same class, a basic result today known as Kleene's Theorem.

claim: Go's regexp package is guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input.
quote: The regexp implementation provided by this package is guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input.
